lines: Take the exact same sequence of updates to one logical record, and apply it three genuinely different real ways: overwrite it where it sits, append each new version to a growing log, or copy the whole page it lives on and swap in the new one.
Start with the first way. Does overwriting a record in place ever leave anything behind to clean up later?
answer: The old bytes are simply gone the moment the new ones land.

lines: Run it for real: overwrite the same record five separate times, in place.
Its own footprint, before and after all five updates, is exactly the same, with nothing extra accumulating anywhere.
Now take those same five updates and apply them a different way: append each new version to a growing log instead, and never touch the old one.
Does the log's own footprint actually grow with every single update?
answer: Nothing old gets thrown away on its own; something else has to come along and do that later.

lines: Run it for real: the log's own footprint genuinely grew with every one of the five updates.
Compacting it afterward threw away every version except the newest, shrinking the footprint right back down.
steps.takeaway: Appending each new version keeps every old one around until a real compaction pass goes and discards it.

lines: Apply the same five updates one more way: copy the whole page the record lives on, write the new version into that copy, and swap it in.
Does this grow the structure by only the record's own handful of bytes each time, the same way the log did?
answer: A whole page gets copied every single time, no matter how small the update actually is.

lines: Run it for real: copying the whole page on every update genuinely grew the structure by one whole page each time, never just the record's own bytes.
steps.takeaway: Copy-on-write own unit of work is the whole page, so its footprint grows by a page each time.

lines: Compare the real amount left behind by the append-only version and the copy-on-write version, on the exact same five updates.
Which one leaves more behind for some later cleanup pass to reclaim?
answer: Every discarded copy there is a whole page, not just one small record.

lines: Run it for real: on the exact same five updates, the copy-on-write version's own leftover was measurably, strictly larger than the append-only version's own leftover.
One real system built around copying pages explains why that larger cost is worth paying: because no active page is ever touched directly, a crash can never leave a page sitting half-written.
There's no special recovery step needed at all afterward, because every page on disk was always either fully old or fully new.
steps.takeaway: Copy-on-write's larger footprint buys crash safety: a page never overwritten can't be left half-written.

lines: So, pulling this topic together: the cheapest choice in space destroys the old version outright the moment it's overwritten.
Keeping every version around costs more, until something comes along and cleans the old ones out.
And paying the most, a whole page at a time, is exactly what buys a page that a crash can never catch half-finished.
